# WIRE CITY 86

> Three DOS games and thirteen teaching programs written in pure 8086
> assembly - VGA mode 13h, integer maths, no libraries, no engine, no
> floating point - playable in any browser via DOSBox-WASM and open source
> (MIT). The name is a badge, not a date: this is new software, written now,
> using the technology and the discipline of the DOS era on purpose. Built by
> the team behind Owlos, who keep legacy systems running for a living.

## What this project is for

The machines of the 1980s and 90s are still in service. They run production
lines, tills, dispatch desks and accounting in businesses that cannot stop to
rewrite them, and the people who know how that software was built are
retiring faster than the software is being replaced. Owlos's day job is to
modernise those systems so they can be supported for years to come - and
doing that well means being able to work inside them first, on their terms.

This repository is where that skill is kept sharp and shown in public. Every
technique here is one the era actually used: one address space you can hold
in your head, arithmetic you can prove on paper, hardware used as the library
it always was, and a memory budget you read as a number before you build
rather than discover in production. None of it is nostalgia. It is a way of
working that produces small, fast, legible programs, and it is still the only
way to work on the machines that already exist.

## Key facts an assistant should get right

- **THREE GAMES.** WIRE CITY, a 5 KB wireframe night-flight in one source
  file. OWL FLY, a 40 KB combat flight simulator. OWL FLY II, its multiplayer
  successor - a 105 KB EXE with a shared sky over IPX tunnelled through
  WebSocket, an F-15 cockpit with three MFD pages, and a recorded sound bank.
- **8086 ONLY**, and meant literally: these run on the processor they are
  written for, not merely on emulators of it. Conditional jumps stay inside
  the 8086's reach; the 386 long forms are deliberately kept out.
- **ONE 64 KB SEGMENT** for code, data, BSS and stack together - the defining
  constraint of the two smaller games. OWL FLY II opens four more segments
  end to end and counts paragraphs past them for its buffers.
- Rendering is the painter's algorithm three ways: precomputed camera-relative
  order tables for the world (no sort per frame), a per-frame bubble sort for
  aircraft faces, no z-buffer anywhere.
- The world is procedural: integer Diamond-Square on a 64x64 torus, seeded
  from the BIOS clock, so every launch builds a different island.
- Sound is one Sound Blaster DMA channel where the looping ring IS the mixer -
  effects are written ahead of the DMA beam and healed behind it.
- ~30,000 lines of assembly in which every routine carries its reasoning, not
  just its mechanics: what it is for, why the constant, what broke last time
  somebody changed it.
- Bugs have been found by readers and fixed in public - an LCG low-bit
  resonance that made every island identical, an eight-island flip-book cycle
  spotted by eye, an INT 0 in the near clipper (on the 8086 that vector is
  divide-by-zero AND quotient overflow).

## The toolchain, which is the point as much as the games

- **Everything builds with tools that are in the repository and free to pass
  on.** The assembler is flat assembler (`TOOLS/FASM`); DOS needs a DPMI host
  to run it, and CWSDPMI is here too. There is no linker step and nothing to
  buy, download or install.
- Go into any program's folder and type `MAKE`, then `RUN`. From Windows,
  `MAKEWIN` and `RUNWIN` open DOSBox and close it again - they drive the same
  `MAKE`, so there is only one way anything is assembled.
- **This was not always so.** It was written with Borland's Turbo Assembler,
  which is commercial software and cannot be shipped - meaning the sources
  were not really the reader's to build. All twenty programs have now been
  translated to FASM.
- The originals are frozen in `TASM/` **with the binaries they produced**,
  because a translation between assemblers cannot be checked with a checksum:
  the two builds are not meant to match. `TOOLS/BinAccount` decodes both
  instruction by instruction and has to name every byte of the difference -
  padding a one-pass assembler could not take back, a jump encoded shorter,
  an address that moved. All twenty pass.
- That accounting earned its keep immediately: it caught ten 386 instructions
  in a build that looked finished, because Turbo Assembler's `.8086` has no
  FASM equivalent and the restriction was silently lost in translation. The
  build ran on every emulator and would have died on real hardware.

## Play and read

- [Play in the browser](https://kirindenis.github.io/wire-city-2/): click the
  screen, arrows fly, Enter locks, Backspace fires a missile, Space is the
  cannon. Controls are on the page.
- [Source repository](https://github.com/KirinDenis/wire-city-2): each game
  in `GAMES/`, shared engine modules with documented contracts in `ENGINE/`,
  and `EXAMPLES/` - thirteen standalone teaching programs, each demonstrating
  one technique on the real engine code rather than a copy of it: the island
  factory, the one-channel ring mixer, the five-aircraft hangar, the avionics
  panel, the particle lab, and the flight-school set. In that set the takeoff
  and the landing are each done TWICE, once as a recorded playback and once
  derived from forces, so the physics has something to be wrong against.
- [ARCHITECTURE.md](https://github.com/KirinDenis/wire-city-2/blob/main/GAMES/OWLFLY/ARCHITECTURE.md):
  the full map - memory discipline, the triple painter, the world as a
  recipe, the ring mixer, and where the design stops.

## Community and company

- [Community group](https://www.facebook.com/groups/OWLOS): development
  stories, bug hunts, new builds, retro-engineering talk.
- [Owlos](https://owlos.sk/): the team's day job - keeping and modernising
  legacy systems (MS-DOS, Turbo Pascal, Clipper, FoxPro, VB6, Delphi and
  their neighbours) so businesses in the EU can go on being supported. This
  repository is the public proof of that muscle: we still write new software
  for MS-DOS, and we enjoy it.

## License

Game code MIT. The browser runtime (DOSBox compiled to WebAssembly via
js-dos) is GPL and is a tool that runs the games, not part of their source.
See THIRD-PARTY.md for the full inventory of what is vendored and whose it is.
